Predictive policing entered mainstream law enforcement practice through foundational overviews like @perry_2013_predictive-policing-role's RAND report, which frames it as analytical techniques for identifying intervention targets, and @bachner_2013_predictive-policing-preventing's practitioner-facing survey of early municipal adoption. Both treat the technology as a tool whose value depends entirely on the quality of the data feeding it and the discretion of the officers acting on its outputs, not as a self-contained solution.

That dependency is the entry point for the critical literature. @crawford-schultz_2014_big-data-due argue that predictive systems trained on historical enforcement data reproduce and legitimize prior policing patterns under the appearance of neutral, data-driven objectivity. They propose a "procedural data due process" grounded in due process's traditional role as a constraint on *adjudication*. If implemented, whenever a Big Data system would be used to determine attributes or categories for an individual, the affected person would have a right to notice and an opportunity to contest that determination. This framing fits person-based systems, like Operation LASER's "Chronic Offender" scoring, more directly than place-based ones like PredPol, where no individual is ever notified or given anything to contest. The harder question their framework raises for a place-based system is who, if anyone, is owed process when a neighborhood rather than a person is the thing being categorized. @lau_2020_predictive-policing-explained's overview for the Brennan Center for Justice synthesizes this critique for a policy audience, cataloging the same feedback-loop and transparency concerns raised elsewhere in this literature [@lum-isaac_2016_to-predict-and-serve].

Evaluations of specific deployments are more mixed than the foundational literature's framing suggests. The Department of Justice's CrimeSolutions program-profile review independently assesses PredPol's Los Angeles deployment [@national-institute-of-justice_2022_predictive-policing-model], a level of formal government evaluation most departments' predictive tools never receive. More recent scholarship situates individual programs like PredPol within a broader political economy of policing: @vargas-etal_2025_political-economy-policing argue that policing institutions are shaped as much by economic and ideological pressures external to crime-fighting as by crime itself, a framing consistent with PredPol's own end, which press coverage attributed to a budget crisis rather than to the accumulated bias critique [@haskins_2020_tool-was-supposed; @cushing_2020_lapds-failed-predictive-policing].

Two things are missing from this literature that this project addresses. First, almost none of it evaluates what happens *after* a predictive policing program is discontinued; the field is oriented around evaluating deployment, not succession. Second, the DICFP-specific claims discussed below have so far been made qualitatively, not tested against tract-level enforcement data.
